claim: All olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) that express the same odorant receptor project their axons to the same antennal-lobe (AL) glomerulus.
source: All olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) that express the same odorant receptor project their axons to the same antennal-lobe (AL) glomerulus.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the convergence of OSNs to glomeruli.

claim: AL projection neurons (PNs) passing along the most prominent tract, the medial AL tract (mALT) have dendrites in a single glomerulus and receive direct input from one OSN class.
source: AL projection neurons (PNs) passing along the most prominent tract, the medial AL tract (mALT) have dendrites in a single glomerulus and receive direct input from one OSN class.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The neuron connectivity in Ca has a semi-random topographical distribution, where signals are segregated according to the nature of sensory input.
source: The neuron connectivity in Ca has a semi-random topographical distribution, where signals are segregated according to the nature of sensory input, for example, pheromone and general odor PNs have their terminals located at the inner and outer part of calyces, respectively (Zhao et al., 2014), but connections between the projection neurons and the Kenyon cells are random (Caron et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Zhao et al., 2014; Caron et al., 2013).

claim: Kenyon cells process signals of positive versus negative valence into different terminal clusters.
source: Instead of encoding the identity of stimuli, the Kenyon cells process signals of positive versus negative valence into different terminal clusters (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014a and 2014b.

claim: The lateral protocerebrum shares many neural principles with the mammalian cortical amygdala.
source: This brain region shares many neural principles with the mammalian cortical amygdala (Miyamichi et al., 2011; Sosulski et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miyamichi et al., 2011 and Sosulski et al., 2011.

claim: Signals inducing different behaviors, such as pheromones versus food odors, are segregated in the lateral protocerebrum both in fruit fly and moths.
source: Signals inducing different behaviors, such as pheromones versus food odors, are segregated in the lateral protocerebrum both in fruit fly and moths (Grabe and Sachse, 2018; Homberg et al., 1988; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In the fruit fly, spatial separation in the lateral protocerebrum includes attractive versus repulsive odor signals.
source: In the fruit fly, such spatial separation is shown to include even attractive versus repulsive odor signals (Grabe and Sachse, 2018; Min et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grabe and Sachse, 2018 and Min et al., 2013.

claim: In Helicoverpa armigera, three male-specific glomeruli receive input about three female-produced signals.
source: In Helicoverpa armigera, three male-specific glomeruli receive input about three female-produced signals, the primary pheromone component, serving as an attractant, and two minor constituents, serving a dual function, that is, attraction versus inhibition of attraction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The medial tract is the most prominent tract conveying information from the MGC to higher olfactory centers.
source: From the antennal-lobe glomeruli, the information is conveyed to higher olfactory centers, including the lateral protocerebrum, via three main paths – of which the medial tract is the most prominent.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and introduction.

claim: The neurons' widespread projections are organized according to behavioral significance, including a spatial separation of signals representing attraction versus inhibition.
source: Our data suggest that the neurons' widespread projections are organized according to behavioral significance, including a spatial separation of signals representing attraction versus inhibition – however, with a unique capacity of switching behavioral consequence based on the amount of the minor components.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: The male moth Helicoverpa armigera utilizes cis-11-hexadecenal (Z11-16:Al) as the primary pheromone component.
source: The male moth studied here, Helicoverpa armigera (Lepidoptera, Noctuidae, Heliothinae), utilizes cis-11-hexadecenal (Z11-16:Al) as the primary pheromone component and cis-9-hexadecenal (Z9-16:Al) as a secondary component (Kehat and Dunkelblum, 1990), in a species-specific ratio ranging from 100:2.5 to 100:4.5 (Berg et al., 2014; Hillier and Baker, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Z9-16:Al is identical with the primary pheromone component of the coresidential and closely related species, Helicoverpa assulta.
source: Notably, the secondary constituent is identical with the primary pheromone component of the coresidential and closely related species, Helicoverpa assulta, in which Z11-16:Al and Z9-16:Al form the pheromone blend in a range of ratios from 5.7:100 to 6.7:100 (Berg et al., 2014; Hillier and Baker, 2016; Wang et al., 2005), and could thus act as an aversive signal at high concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Z9-14:Al acts as a behavioral antagonist inhibiting pheromone attraction when more than five units are added to 100 units of the specific binary pheromone blend.
source: At higher dosages, it acts as a behavioral antagonist inhibiting the pheromone attraction, that is, when more than five units of Z9-14:Al are added to 100 units of the specific binary pheromone blend (Gothilf et al., 1978; Kehat and Dunkelblum, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Z9-14:Al acts as an agonist when 0.3–5 units are added to 100 units of the specific binary pheromone blend.
source: However, at lower dosages, it acts as an agonist, that is, when 0.3–5 units are added to 100 units of the specific binary pheromone blend (Wu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: The MGC comprises three units in H. armigera: cumulus, dorsomedial posterior (dmp) unit, and dorsomedial anterior (dma) unit.
source: In the species used here, H. armigera, the MGC comprises three units (Skiri et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2016) receiving input from three OSN categories: (1) the cumulus from OSNs tuned to the primary component, Z11-16:Al, (2) the dorsomedial posterior (dmp) unit from OSNs tuned mainly to the secondary component, Z9-16:Al, and (3) the dorsomedial anterior (dma) unit from OSNs tuned to the behavioral antagonist/enhancer, Z9-14:AL (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and calcium imaging data in Figure 2.

claim: The cumulus receives input from OSNs tuned to the primary component, Z11-16:Al.
source: the cumulus from OSNs tuned to the primary component, Z11-16:Al
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2.

claim: The dmp unit receives input from OSNs tuned mainly to the secondary component, Z9-16:Al.
source: the dorsomedial posterior (dmp) unit from OSNs tuned mainly to the secondary component, Z9-16:Al
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2.

claim: The dma unit receives input from OSNs tuned to the behavioral antagonist/enhancer, Z9-14:Al.
source: the dorsomedial anterior (dma) unit from OSNs tuned to the behavioral antagonist/enhancer, Z9-14:AL (Wu et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2.

claim: The average correlation between the cumulus medial-tract PNs responses across individuals was 0.45.
source: The average correlation between the cumulus medial-tract PNs responses (mean calcium signal during stimulation windows subtracted by that during the pre-stimulation period) across individuals was 0.45.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The average correlations of PNs from the dma and dmp units across individuals were 0.55 and 0.24, respectively.
source: The corresponding average correlations of PNs from the dma and dmp units were 0.55 and 0.24, respectively (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The cumulus PN population showed a pronounced activation during stimulation with the primary pheromone and the pheromone blend.
source: As expected, the cumulus PN population showed a pronounced activation during stimulation with the primary pheromone and the pheromone blend.
evidence: This is shown in the calcium imaging data in Figure 2E.

claim: The dma output neuron population responded to the behavioral antagonist, the primary pheromone, and the pheromone blend.
source: The dma output neuron population, in turn, responded not only to the behavioral antagonist but also to the primary pheromone and the pheromone blend.
evidence: This is shown in the calcium imaging data in Figure 2E.

claim: The dmp PNs responded to the secondary pheromone, the behavioral antagonist, and the pheromone mixture.
source: The dmp PNs responded to the secondary pheromone and the behavioral antagonist, as well as to the pheromone mixture.
evidence: This is shown in the calcium imaging data in Figure 2E.

claim: 32 PNs were recorded across 32 preparations.
source: We recorded 32 PNs across 32 preparations (Figure 3A–F, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2 and Videos 1–10).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the intracellular recording experiments.

claim: 29 PNs were confined to the mALT and three to the mlALT.
source: Among them, 29 PNs were confined to the prominent mALT and three to the substantially thinner mlALT (the morphological features of individual neurons are summarized in Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the intracellular recording experiments.

claim: Uniglomerular medial-tract MGC-PNs projected sparsely to a restricted area in the inner layer of the calycal cups before targeting at least one of four regions in the lateral protocerebrum.
source: Generally, the uniglomerular medial-tract MGC-PNs projected sparsely to a restricted area in the inner layer of the calycal cups before targeting at least one of four regions in the lateral protocerebrum, that is, the ventrolateral protocerebrum (VLP), the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP), the anteroventral lateral horn (LH), and the posterodorsal part of the superior intermediate protocerebrum (SIP) (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The three MGC-PNs following the mediolateral ALT were multiglomerular and projected directly to the lateral protocerebrum without innervating the calyces.
source: The three MGC-PNs following the mediolateral ALT were multiglomerular and projected directly to the lateral protocerebrum without innervating the calyces (Figure 3A,E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The VLP receives projections from all MGC output neurons.
source: the VLP for all MGC output neurons
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The SLP and SIP receive projections from PNs innervating cumulus.
source: the SLP and SIP for PNs innervating cumulus
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The LH receives projections from PNs originating from each of the two smaller MGC units as well as multiglomerular medial-tract PNs arborizing in the whole MGC.
source: the LH for PNs originating from each of the two smaller MGC units as well as multiglomerular medial-tract PNs arborizing in the whole MGC
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The primary pheromone signals were processed within the SLP and SIP whereas the minor components were represented in the LH.
source: The primary pheromone signals were processed within the SLP and SIP whereas the minor components were represented in the LH.
evidence: This is stated in the Results based on the descriptive framework in Figure 3G.

claim: The simulation was consistent with the recorded data, demonstrated by strong correlations between the simulated and recorded neural activities across the four different odors (R2 > 0.6).
source: The simulation was consistent with the recorded data, demonstrated by strong correlations between the simulated and recorded neural activities across the four different odors (R2 > 0.6, Figure 3H2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 3H2.

claim: PNs confined to the medial and mediolateral tract overlapped in the VLP.
source: PNs confined to the medial and mediolateral tract, however, overlapped in the VLP (dashed circle in Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the multi-staining experiment in Figure 4A.

claim: The cumulus PNs commonly responded with increased spiking frequency to both low and high concentrations of the primary pheromone and the pheromone mixture.
source: The cumulus PNs commonly responded with increased spiking frequency to both low and high concentrations of the primary pheromone and the pheromone mixture (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiological data in Figure 5 and supplements.

claim: The phasic onset was most prominent for PNs in the low concentration protocol.
source: The phasic onset was most prominent for PNs in the low concentration protocol (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Cumulus-PNs in the low concentration protocol appeared to discriminate between odorants more precisely than PNs in the high concentration protocol.
source: these neurons also appeared to discriminate between odorants more precisely than PNs in the high concentration protocol (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E.

claim: OSNs display less specific response profiles with increasing odor concentrations.
source: This coincides with previous studies reporting that OSNs display less specific response profiles with increasing odor concentrations (Malnic et al., 1999; Sato et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Uniglomerular dma PNs having fine branches approaching the SLP in addition to the terminals in the VLP and LH were excited by the behavioral antagonist and the secondary pheromone.
source: PNs having fine branches approaching the SLP in addition to the terminals in the VLP and LH, were excited by the behavioral antagonist and the secondary pheromone (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A–C)
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiological data in Figure 5—figure supplement 4A–C.

claim: Uniglomerular dma PNs with restricted projections in the VLP and LH were not excited by the behavioral antagonist.
source: while PNs with restricted projections in the VLP and LH were not (Figure 5—figure supplement 4D–F)
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiological data in Figure 5—figure supplement 4D–F.

claim: Only one of the dmp-PNs was significantly excited by both the secondary pheromone and the behavioral antagonist.
source: Even though the dmp unit reportedly receives input about the secondary pheromone and the behavioral antagonist (Wu et al., 2015), only one of the dmp-PNs identified here was significantly excited by both of these components (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiological data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The two mlALT PNs projecting to the VLP exclusively were more broadly tuned by responding with excitation to all stimuli.
source: The other sub-type, including two mlALT PNs, projecting to the VLP exclusively, covered the MGC units quite uniformly. These PNs were more broadly tuned by responding with excitation to all stimuli.
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiological data in Figure 5—figure supplement 7.

claim: The responses of mlALT PNs to the pheromone mixture and the primary pheromone lasted substantially longer than the phasic excitations elicited by the secondary component and the behavioral antagonist.
source: However, their responses to the pheromone mixture and the primary pheromone lasted substantially longer than the phasic excitations elicited by the secondary component and the behavioral antagonist (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiological data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 7.

claim: mALT PNs with dendrites in the cumulus deal with the primary pheromone.
source: The mean responses within the different neuron groups showed that mALT PNs with dendrites in the cumulus deal with the primary pheromone
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A summarizing the electrophysiological responses.

claim: mALT PNs with dendrites in the dmp unit deal with the secondary pheromone and the behavioral antagonist.
source: and those in the dmp unit with the secondary pheromone and the behavioral antagonist
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A summarizing the electrophysiological responses.

claim: Both individual PN recordings and calcium imaging tests indicated a role for the dma PNs in processing information about the behavioral antagonist, the primary pheromone, and pheromone mixture.
source: However, unlike previous reports on OSN input, both our individual PN recordings and calcium imaging tests indicated a role for the dma PNs in processing information not only about the behavioral antagonist, but also, surprisingly, about the primary pheromone and pheromone mixture.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2 and 6.

claim: The most potent stimuli for uniglomerular dma neurons were the behavioral antagonist and the pheromone mixture.
source: However, averaging the activity across the uniglomerular dma neurons demonstrated that the most potent stimuli for these PNs were the behavioral antagonist and the pheromone mixture, while the primary pheromone elicited only minor increases in mean firing rates.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The multiglomerular mALT and mlALT PNs arborizing in the entire MGC were activated by all female-produced components.
source: For the fourth group, which consisted of the multiglomerular mALT and mlALT PNs arborizing in the entire MGC, the averaged data demonstrated activation by all female-produced components.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The lateral protocerebrum contributes to innate attraction/avoidance behavior based on composite odor input coding.
source: Taken together, these results confirm our previous suggestions signifying that the lateral protocerebrum contributes to innate attraction/avoidance behavior based on composite odor input coding (Chu et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion supported by the current data and previous work.

claim: The moth has three main tracts connecting the lateral protocerebrum and the AL.
source: Similar to the most studied insect model, the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, the moth also has three main tracts connecting the lateral protocerebrum and the AL.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both medial- and lateral-tract MGC-PNs are mainly uniglomerular.
source: Interestingly, both medial- and lateral-tract MGC-PNs are mainly uniglomerular.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the current and previous data.

claim: The medial tract includes PNs originating from each of the three MGC-units whereas the lateral tract is reported to connect with the cumulus exclusively.
source: However, the medial tract includes PNs originating from each of the three MGC-units whereas the lateral tract is reported to connect with the cumulus exclusively.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the current data and previous work (Chu et al., 2020a).

claim: Medial-tract MGC-PNs extend widespread terminal branches into various protocerebral regions, including the SLP, posterior SIP, and VLP.
source: while medial-tract MGC-PNs extend widespread terminal branches into various protocerebral regions, including the SLP, posterior SIP, and VLP
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 7.

claim: The (unilateral) lateral-tract MGC-PNs converge within a restricted region anteriorly in the SIP called the column.
source: the (unilateral) lateral-tract MGC-PNs converge within a restricted region anteriorly in the SIP called the column (Chu et al., 2020a)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on previous work.

claim: The assembly of 42 MGC-PNs covers every previously reported MGC neuron type in heliothine moths.
source: This assembly covers every previously reported MGC neuron type in heliothine moths (Berg et al., 1998; Christensen et al., 1991; Christensen et al., 1995; Ian et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019; Vickers et al., 1998; Zhao and Berg, 2010; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The proportion of sampled neurons originating from each of the MGC units is in high correspondence with the volume of the relevant MGC unit.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the proportion of sampled neurons originating from each of the MGC units is in high correspondence with the volume of the relevant MGC unit (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The excitatory response to the pheromone mixture arose first in the SIP, as a typical phasic response.
source: Here, the excitatory response to the pheromone mixture arose first in the SIP, as a typical phasic response.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the temporal response framework in Figure 7C.

claim: After 20 ms, a phasic-tonic response to the binary mixture appeared in the SLP and VLP.
source: After 20 ms, a phasic-tonic response to the binary mixture appeared in the SLP and VLP.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the temporal response framework in Figure 7C.

claim: About 120 ms after the initial response, a weak signal lasting for 10 ms could be seen in the LH.
source: Finally, about 120 ms later, a weak signal lasting for 10 ms could be seen in the LH.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the temporal response framework in Figure 7C.

claim: The lateral-tract PNs react prior to PNs in the other main tracts.
source: Comparing the response onset in the SIP with the other output regions, demonstrates that the lateral-tract PNs react prior to PNs in the other main tracts (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The MGC neurons confined to medial tract in H. armigera have a much lower spontaneous firing rate as compared with the lateral-tract PNs.
source: This is particularly interesting as the MGC neurons confined to medial tract in this species have a much lower spontaneous firing rate as compared with the lateral-tract PNs (Chu et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The 'quieter' background of the medial-tract PNs might facilitate registration of the pheromone signals.
source: The 'quieter' background of the medial-tract PNs might facilitate registration of the pheromone signals.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion.

claim: The medial-tract PNs to a large extent are wired with OSNs indirectly via local interneurons, while the lateral-tract PNs may have synaptic contact more directly with the OSNs.
source: One possible explanation for this property could be that the medial-tract PNs to a large extent are wired with OSNs indirectly via local interneurons, while the lateral-tract PNs may have synaptic contact more directly with the OSNs.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion.

claim: In the fruit fly, local interneurons have stronger connections with the mALT PNs than the lALT PNs in the sexually dimorphic glomerulus VA1v.
source: This coincides with the connectomical results shown for the sexually dimorphic glomerulus, VA1v, in the fruit fly, where the local interneurons have stronger connections with the mALT PNs than the lALT PNs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Horne et al., 2018.

claim: The number of presynaptic sites is much higher in the medial-tract PNs than in the lateral-tract PNs in the fruit fly.
source: Besides, the number of presynaptic sites is much higher in the medial-tract PNs than in the lateral-tract PNs, and the dendritic arborizations are also denser in the medial-tract PNs (Horne et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Horne et al., 2018.

claim: The mALT and mlALT are involved in fine-tuned odor coding, whereas the lALT plays a different role by initiating flight behavior evoked by the key component.
source: This reinforces our proposed concept implying that the mALT and mlALT are involved in fine-tuned odor coding, whereas the lALT plays a different role by initiating flight behavior evoked by the key component (Chu et al., 2020a; Ian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion based on the current data and previous work.

claim: All uniglomerular mALT PNs innervating the SLP and SIP had their dendrites in the cumulus.
source: All uniglomerular mALT PNs innervating the SLP and SIP had their dendrites in the cumulus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the morphological data.

claim: The cumulus-PNs responded mainly to the primary pheromone.
source: These cumulus-PNs responded mainly to the primary pheromone.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: Third-order pheromone-processing neurons in the SLP and SIP should primarily be involved in computations related to attraction.
source: Thus, third-order pheromone-processing neurons in the SLP and SIP should primarily be involved in computations related to attraction.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference based on the data.

claim: The anteroventral LH was the target for the PNs originating in one of the two smaller MGC units, the dma and dmp.
source: In contrast to the SLP and SIP, being innervated by the medial-tract cumulus neurons, the anteroventral LH was the target for the PNs originating in one of the two smaller MGC units, the dma and dmp.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the morphological data.

claim: Input about the primary pheromone is processed dorsomedially to input about the secondary component and the behavioral antagonist.
source: Thereby, input about the primary pheromone is processed dorsomedially to input about the secondary component and the behavioral antagonist.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference based on the spatial organization.

claim: This lateral-medial separation resembles the spatial pattern previously reported in the closely related species, H. assulta.
source: This lateral-medial separation resembles the spatial pattern previously reported in the closely related species, H. assulta, where the primary pheromone is represented medially to the interspecific signal (Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: The highest mean firing rate in the LH appeared during application of the behavioral antagonist.
source: Summarizing the response patterns of the MGC-PNs innervating the LH (Figure 7C), we found that the highest mean firing rate appeared during application of the behavioral antagonist.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on Figure 7C.

claim: Z9-14:Al reduces mating-associated behaviors as soon as its ratio vs. binary pheromone blend increases to 5:100.
source: As mentioned in the introduction, the behavioral antagonist, Z9-14:Al, reduces mating-associated behaviors as soon as its ratio vs. binary pheromone blend increases to 5:100 (Kehat and Dunkelblum, 1990; Wu et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Z9-14:Al enhances mating-associated behaviors when the ratio is between 0.3:100 and 5:100.
source: while it enhances such behaviors when the ratio is between 0.3:100 and 5:100 (Wu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: A small amount of Z9-14:Al is released by H. armigera females (ratio of Z9-14:Al to Z11-16:Al is 0.3:100).
source: Indeed, a small amount of this component, Z9-14:Al, is released by H. armigera females (ratio of Z9-14:Al to Z11-16:Al is 0.3:100; Kehat and Dunkelblum, 1990; Zhang et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Sympatric Heliothis peltigera females emit a higher amount of Z9-14:Al (ratio of Z9-14:Al to Z11-16:Al is 14.6:100).
source: while sympatric Heliothis peltigera females emit a higher amount of the same component (ratio of Z9-14:Al to Z11-16:Al is 14.6:100; see Hillier and Baker, 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: Z9-16:Al augments attraction when combined with the primary pheromone Z11-16:Al.
source: Concretely, Z9-16:Al is known to augment attraction when combined with the primary pheromone Z11-16:Al, but to reduce attraction when constituting a ratio to primary pheromone more than 11:100 (Kehat and Dunkelblum, 1990; Kehat et al., 1980).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Z9-16:Al reduces attraction when constituting a ratio to primary pheromone more than 11:100.
source: but to reduce attraction when constituting a ratio to primary pheromone more than 11:100 (Kehat and Dunkelblum, 1990; Kehat et al., 1980)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: High ratios of Z9-16:Al may serve as an interspecific signal, due to it being the primary pheromone of sympatric H. assulta females.
source: Notably, high ratios of Z9-16:Al may serve as an interspecific signal, due to it being the primary pheromone of sympatric H. assulta females (Cork et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: The anteroventral part of the LH is involved in inhibition of attraction when the moth encounters high ratios of the relevant components.
source: Altogether, in light of the complex behavioral functions of Z9-16:Al and Z9-14:Al, our data indicate that the anteroventral part of the LH is involved in inhibition of attraction when the moth encounters high ratios of the relevant components.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion based on the data and behavioral context.

claim: A prominent neural link exists between the LH and SLP in moths.
source: Notably, a prominent neural link between the LH and SLP in moths (Namiki and Kanzaki, 2019) appears to be a strong candidate for governing the 'correct' mate-searching behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: The LH output in the fruit fly projects primarily to SLP and secondly to the SIP.
source: A study in the fruit fly has demonstrated that the LH output projects primarily to SLP and secondly to the SIP, and about one-third of these neurons are GABAergic/glutamatergic (Dolan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: About one-third of LH output neurons in the fruit fly are GABAergic/glutamatergic.
source: and about one-third of these neurons are GABAergic/glutamatergic (Dolan et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: Both GABA and glutamate are inhibitory neurotransmitters in insects.
source: Since both neurotransmitters are inhibitory (Liu and Wilson, 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: LH input may block the activation of SLP and SIP output neurons and their downstream circuits.
source: this indicates that LH input may block the activation of SLP and SIP output neurons and their downstream circuits
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference based on the neurotransmitter properties.

claim: The interaction between the LH and SLP/SIP could act as a Boolean logic gate implementing the AND-NOT function.
source: The interaction between the LH and SLP/SIP could act as a Boolean logic gate implementing the AND-NOT function, only passing information downstream when aversive signaling is minimally present in the anteroventral LH.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed model.

claim: The activity of AL PNs increases with increasing odor concentration.
source: The LH output is mainly modulated by the input from the AL PNs, and the activity of these neurons increases with increasing odor concentration (Gupta and Stopfer, 2012; Lerner et al., 2020; Sachse and Galizia, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: When a moth encounters the primary pheromone and a very low amount of the secondary pheromone, the LH input is weak and the inhibition from the LH to SLP/SIP minimal.
source: When a moth encounters the primary pheromone and a very low amount of the secondary pheromone (released by conspecific female), the LH input is weak and the inhibition from the LH to SLP/SIP minimal, therefore, the output from the SLP/SIP to downstream targets remains strong.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as part of the proposed model.

claim: A big amount of the secondary pheromone or the behavioral antagonist will recruit vigorous MGC-PN output onto the LH.
source: Should a big amount of the secondary pheromone or the behavioral antagonist (released by a heterospecific female) recruit vigorous MGC-PN output onto the LH, the GABAergic/glutamatergic LH neurons will inhibit the activity in SLP/SIP and the downstream signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as part of the proposed model.

claim: Loss of contact with the primary pheromone leads the moth to quickly engage in a casting flight.
source: This might be perceived as a loss of contact with the primary pheromone, leading the moth to quickly engage in a casting flight, that is, crosswind flight with no net upwind movement (Kuenen and Cardé, 1994), and thereby promote an appropriate mate-searching strategy.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as part of the proposed model and supported by citation.

claim: Integration of the secondary and primary pheromone might occur at the level of MGC output PNs.
source: Concerning Z9-16:Al, for example, our findings indicate that integration of the secondary and primary pheromone might occur at the level of MGC output PNs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference based on the data.

claim: The pheromone mixture showed a tendency of evoking a stronger response than the primary pheromone alone in cumulus PNs.
source: In both electrophysiological recording and calcium imaging experiments, the pheromone mixture showed a tendency of evoking a stronger response (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: At least three cumulus-PNs with projections in the SLP had a tonic and delayed excitation to the secondary pheromone.
source: We also found at least three cumulus-PNs with projections in the SLP that had a tonic and delayed excitation to the secondary pheromone (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3G) suggesting the existence of local computation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3G.

claim: The VLP was innervated by all MGC-PNs labelled in this study.
source: Unlike the neuropils discussed above, the VLP was innervated by all MGC-PNs labelled in this study.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the morphological data.

claim: The VLP gets intermingled signals about all female-relevant compounds.
source: Specifically, they sent terminal projections into a compact sub-domain of the dorsoanterior VLP, which thereby gets intermingled signals about all female-relevant compounds.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the morphological and physiological data.

claim: The VLP is involved in combinatorial coding, possibly recognizing the optimal species-specific signal.
source: This suggests that the VLP is involved in combinatorial coding, possibly recognizing the optimal species-specific signal.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference based on the data.

claim: About half of the axons forming the mediolateral tract are GABAergic.
source: These PNs responded to all female-produced components, but with distinct temporal patterns (Figure 7), and may provide excitatory or inhibitory output since about half of the axons forming this tract are GABAergic (Berg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: The mlALT PNs had overlapping terminals with the medial-tract MGC-PNs in the VLP.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that these mlALT PNs had overlapping terminals with the medial-tract MGC-PNs in this neuropil (Figure 4A), indicating the possibility of axo-axonic interaction.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The VLP is one known region with overlapping terminals of pheromone PNs across different tracts.
source: As the VLP is one known region with overlapping terminals of pheromone PNs across different tracts, this makes it a particularly interesting neuropil for future studies investigating parallel processing in the pheromone system.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion based on the data.
